summary: Introduced the in-app changelog
details: Created a bundled changelog data file and modal so players can review product updates from the account bar.

summary: Introduced the expandable player menu
details: Refined the new account menu into a compact, file-menu inspired widget with role badges, uppercase player names, and a slim character/chronicle/location strip while keeping the changelog button separate.

summary: Restored chronicle list API calls
details: Hardened the Lambda handlers so API Gateway requests without the HTTP v2 metadata stop crashing, which restores the listCharacters and listChronicles player flows.

summary: Refined UI styling and menus
details: Collapsed the recent CSS refactors, player menu polish, character panel updates, and template shortcut tweaks into a single styling refresh that keeps the UI consistent.

summary: Added the moderator LLM audit review workspace
details: Moderators and admins can open the new LLM audit review page from the player menu to filter archived LLM requests, capture structured review notes, and inspect template improvement proposals.

summary: Rolled out moderator world graph maintenance
details: Moderators and admins can use the World Atlas from the player menu to browse shared entities, edit hard-state metadata, and manage canonical graph relationships.

summary: Stabilized LLM proxy requests
details: Typed the chronicle API's LLM client against the proxy schema, added JSON coercion heuristics for fenced or double-encoded responses, and automatically retries the proxy when parsing still fails.

summary: Players can react to GM stories
details: Added a Give Feedback button to GM replies so players can share a quick sentiment and note. Submissions piggyback on the audit API so moderators see feedback alongside narrative request logs.

summary: Players can request chronicle endings
details: Added a Wrap Up toggle next to Send to GM that stores a chronicle targetEndTurn marker and updates the narrative prompting so the GM closes the story within three turns when requested.

summary: Wrap-up turns now end chronicles
details: GM summaries now emit JSON with a closure signal, so once the story lands the chronicle flips to closed, the API blocks more turns, and the client disables Send/Wrap for that session.

summary: Chronicle beats anchor long-term goals
details: Chronicle creation now lets you enable beat tracking (on by default), the GM automatically seeds and resolves beats with title/description/status updates, and the client surfaces active beats under the navigation so players can see which story arcs are in progress.

summary: Chronicle closures now generate epilogues
details: When a chronicle is closed we enqueue the chronicle-closer Lambda to generate a short-story recap and character bio note via SQS, then persist both as closure summaries without publishing live-session changes into shared world state.

summary: Moderators can triage bug reports
details: Added a bug moderation workspace with a MUI data grid and modal so admins can review every bug report, capture backlog labels, add internal notes, and update the bug store status without leaving the client.

summary: GM turns now adapt to six intent styles
details: The narrative engine now classifies each player message as an action, inquiry, clarification, possibility check, planning beat, or reflection, branches through a new decision-graph, renders dedicated prompt templates, and only applies world deltas when the turn truly advances time. The chat UI now surfaces intent/timeline badges plus world-change traces so players can see how each response impacted the story.

summary: Intent DAG now uses dedicated classifiers
details: Split the router into intent, beat, and skill detector nodes that run gpt-5-nano through the revamped llmResolver, rewrote every prompt template (especially intent intake) to match the new DAG contracts, documented the node/parameter flow in apps/chronicle-api/src/langGraph/README.md, and migrated the llm proxy plus client to the OpenAI responses API with reasoning/text knobs so classifier nodes stay lean.

summary: Landing briefs, player guide, and bug reporting
details: Added a briefing-style landing page with news, recent features, global chronicle signals, and a quick-continue panel so players see what's new before diving in. Chronicle chat now lives at /chron/:id with route-driven hydration, plus a new in-app player guide, live token-usage readout, and system bug report modal so players can find help or flag issues without leaving the client.

summary: Player menu now shows LLM token usage
details: Wired the chronicle API Lambda to the LLM proxy's DynamoDB usage table and granted it read access, so the player menu widget can finally show per-login token consumption instead of an empty state. Also simplified the UI to a compact table with shorthand headers so the stats sit cleanly inside the player menu.

summary: GM API now handles player intents
details: Refactored the client’s send-and-wrap flows and updated the API Gateway/Lambda wiring so player turns now hit the dedicated gm-api while the chronicle service continues handling directory and setup endpoints.

summary: Worldstate moved to Postgres
details: Replaced the hybrid S3/Dynamo persistence layer with a unified Postgres worldstate service, added a property-graph schema for chronicles, characters, turns, and locations, and wired the dev stack plus Terraform to provision and seed a shared RDS instance.

summary: Player identity replaces login everywhere
details: Removed the legacy login table and login identifiers across the stack, rewired DTOs, audits, persistence, APIs, and the client to use player IDs exclusively, and cleaned up front-end flows and tooling to stop mapping between login and player fields.

summary: Retired the legacy persistence package
details: Moved prompt template, audit, and support data into the Postgres-backed stack, split bug reports and token usage into a dedicated ops module with its own migrations, removed the deprecated S3/Dynamo persistence layer (including the usage DynamoDB table), and pointed every API at the new canonical storage modules.

summary: Prompt templates now live in the app schema
details: Introduced the @glass-frontier/app package with its own Postgres schema for players and prompt templates, seeded official template bodies via migrations, removed the S3 prompt bucket dependency, and rewired the APIs to resolve templates and player settings through the new Postgres-backed app store.

summary: Characters now persist full state in Postgres
details: Extended the worldstate character table to store archetype, pronouns, bio, attributes, skills, inventory, and momentum as jsonb fields so the Postgres-backed worldstate stays aligned with the Character DTO instead of only keeping name metadata.

summary: Location graph simplified onto Postgres edges
details: Rebuilt the location schema as a thin table plus graph edges with a single-parent constraint, removed the legacy location-root path columns, and rewired the worldstate location store to use recursive CTEs instead of the custom locationGraph store.

summary: GM API now targets the new location contract
details: Migrated the GM service to the new location contract by consuming the location details query, mapping it back to the existing UI shape, applying location moves through the canonical upsert/edge mutators, and exposing both legacy and new endpoints on the location API during the transition.

summary: World hard state and lore fragments persist in Postgres
details: Seeded world kind/subkind/status and relationship rules from the shared world schema into Postgres, enforced typed hard-state links, and added lore fragment storage plus integration tests so narrative entities and their edges stay consistent.

summary: World schema editor and API
details: Added a moderation page to manage world kinds, subkinds, statuses, and relationship rules, plus a dedicated world-schema API that surfaces the schema and allows updates backed by database constraints.

summary: World Atlas with anchored chronicles
details: Introduced the World Atlas wiki page for entities with editable hard state, relations, and lore, added anchor-aware chronicles via Atlas API, and exposed narrative anchor fragments to the GM prompts for better cohesion.

summary: Hard state prominence levels
details: Hard state entities now carry a five-level prominence field (forgotten → mythic) with slug-based lookups, allowing filtering by prominence and slug-friendly Atlas/chronicle links.

summary: Chronicle seeds now use app prompt templates
details: Seed generation now resolves the chronicle-seed prompt through the app template manager (including player overrides) and removes the legacy local template path so Lambda never looks for bundled prompt files.

summary: GM API timeout increased
details: Extended the GM API Lambda timeout to five minutes so longer narrative runs can complete without timing out.

summary: HTTP APIs now run behind an ALB
details: Replaced API Gateway with an ALB protected by Cognito auth so the HTTP Lambdas keep the same routes while supporting longer timeouts.

summary: Fixed authenticated API CORS preflight failures
details: Corrected malformed origin allowlists in the chronicle and GM Lambda handlers, updated all API Lambdas to emit ALB-compatible 204 preflight payloads with explicit bodies/encoding metadata, switched ALB listener auth from cookie-based authenticate-cognito to strict bearer-token jwt-validation (access tokens only), enabled listener-level CORS response headers, moved API clients to send access tokens in Authorization headers, normalized ALB multiValueHeaders into standard headers before tRPC request planning so authenticated calls stop failing with 502 host-header adapter crashes, and normalized ALB query parameters (including URL-decoding encoded ALB values) before tRPC request planning so batched requests no longer fail with "No procedure found" or "%7B... is not valid JSON" errors.

summary: Restored the paused development baseline
details: Repaired the workspace checks, local build, and full browser harness; enforced access-token identity and ownership across APIs; made live character and location changes chronicle-scoped; committed each narrative turn atomically; completed closure-summary persistence; aligned moderator audit, World Atlas, and world-schema controls with their canonical contracts; and replaced the obsolete bulk world seed with a deterministic local fixture containing three entities, two lore fragments, and one playable chronicle.

summary: Updated models and provider contracts
details: Replaced the stale model list with GPT-5.6, Claude Sonnet 5, Amazon Nova Pro, and Amazon Nova 2 Lite; centralized model IDs, limits, capabilities, and pricing in one catalog; routed Claude through Amazon Bedrock instead of a separate Anthropic API connection; and retained model-specific reasoning and structured-output contracts.

summary: Rebuilt the world graph around one writer and one per-turn read
details: The world vocabulary now lives in a single versioned artifact that the validators, the database seed, and ingest all read, replacing a root JSON file and a duplicate set of hand-written enums; the generic 'related_to' link is banned so every relationship states an actual fact. Canon is written only by validated batches that commit entities, relationships, and lore together and can be reverted whole, replacing per-entity editing that silently reversed a saved entity's incoming relationships. The Atlas and world-schema pages are now readers. Choosing what the GM knows each turn is a single ranked query that walks relationships by strength, so a defining connection reaches further than an incidental one, replacing roughly twenty separate lookups per turn.

summary: Simplified where a chronicle is to a place name
details: A chronicle now tracks where it is as a name, plus the canon place it started from when it started from one. After each turn the game master answers one question about location — did the scene move, and what is it called — instead of matching the answer against the world map, inventing places on it, or working out how places connect. What the world knows about the surroundings still reaches the storyteller, through the same ranked selection that supplies everything else. The location display shows the current place and links to the Atlas only while the chronicle is still where it began.

summary: Fixed GM turn results being silently discarded
details: Turn pipeline steps that run in parallel could overwrite each other's results: the beat a player was advancing, the decision to close a chronicle, and updates to which entities are in focus were all being lost. Pipeline steps now report only what they changed, so parallel results always survive. Several GM prompts were also realigned with the data the game actually expects — the intent classifier and beat detector now describe the real output fields, the inventory arbiter no longer contradicts itself about inventing items, narration prompts can address the character by name, and the risk arbiter sees recent events and the current location when judging a check.

summary: Repaired the play loop from chronicle start through wrap-up
details: Story beats now actually advance and resolve: the GM sees each beat's real identifier, resolutions are recorded permanently, and the beat list you see is the one the server saved. A new chronicle now starts at the location you picked instead of a name invented from the title, and the tone you choose in the wizard follows the whole chronicle into every narration. Wrapping up now guarantees an ending within the next three turns, including when requested before the first turn. While the GM works you see which step of the turn it is on instead of a generic spinner, the pipeline survives sign-in refreshes, and a failed send no longer breaks live updates for the rest of the session. The seed that opened your chronicle stays at the top of the transcript, the anchor step is optional, choosing a generated seed now wins over leftover custom text as the summary shows, and a finished chronicle says plainly that its story is complete.

summary: Let local lore reach the table
details: The world now knows about creatures — animals and anomalies with their own statuses and relationships, including attunement and dependency verbs drawn from the incoming setting's own facts — so imported lore that leans on wildlife arrives intact. Retrieval no longer hides local color: the GM's per-turn world knowledge includes marginal entities (interiors, residents, minor artifacts), keeps their descriptions alongside their lore excerpts, and walks outward from wherever the scene currently is whenever that place matches canon. Stepping inside a named interior therefore keeps its contents in reach. The chronicle wizard also accepts neighboring locations as anchors, so places whose only local support is another place are no longer anchorless.

summary: World schema now mirrors the lore source
details: The game's world vocabulary is now derived directly from the canon source's schema instead of a hand-invented one: its eighteen atlas kinds (abilities, concepts, cultures, eras, incidents, installations, phenomena, species, and more) with their full subkind lists, its complete relation taxonomy including resonance attunement and the DM-only edges, and its declared tag vocabulary, which lore is now validated against. Entities carry their fact cards (born, population, function) into the GM's context, relations keep the in-world years they held, and statuses are free text since the source declares none. Chronicle locations span both natural geography and built installations.

summary: Prepared Glass Frontier for Ahara deployment
details: Glass Frontier now deploys at glass-frontier.com through the shared Ahara network and application load balancer, with no API Gateway or project-owned network infrastructure. Turn progress is retained briefly and polled through an authenticated shared-ALB route. Game data lives in a dedicated logical database on the shared PostgreSQL service, with bounded application connections so play cannot exhaust the platform database.

summary: The Kaleidos system's full canon is now imported
details: The world graph now carries the complete Glass Frontier canon from its authored source, including fact cards, dated relationships, typed GM guidance, and lore spanning settlements, stations, factions, creatures, incidents, and the people of the shattered ring. The Atlas, chronicle wizard, and the GM's per-turn context all draw from this material. Chronicle openings now offer at least ten local choices drawn from people, artifacts, abilities, creatures, transports, cultures, resources, events, and every other non-location kind instead of a mechanically named NPC roster. Deployment loads this production dataset separately from test fixtures and validates the exact shipped artifact before release. Later source revisions reconcile against the imported snapshot while preserving material created through play.

summary: A crisper, denser application shell
details: The portal now fills the whole window like an application instead of floating as a rounded card: a slim top bar carries the wordmark, bug reports, the guide, and the player menu, while each page scrolls inside its own panel. The landing page traded its hero banner for a compact dashboard of characters, chronicles, recent releases, and completed runs. The chat canvas stretches to use the full height of the screen, the chronicle wizard gained a numbered stepper, and panels, chips, and buttons across the app were tightened onto hairline borders and smaller corners to match the turn view's density. Also fixed the composer's screen-reader label rendering as visible text and the unstyled refresh button on the World Atlas.

summary: Chronicle responses now follow player intent and established events
details: New chronicles begin with a generated scene instead of presenting the selected seed as GM dialogue. Intent and beat decisions now use the recent turn record, narration stays in second person without adding actions or possessions for the player, check outcomes carry the planned advantage state, and closing summaries no longer invent travel or lasting character changes.

summary: The World Atlas is now an actual atlas
details: The Atlas opens on a true top-down chart of the Kaleidos system drawn from canon's authored spatial geometry: the sun at center, each planet on its declared orbit rank at its declared angle, moons beside their primaries, trade lanes drawn through their authored waypoints, and deep-space objects like Hinge Six charted as free markers. Clicking a body drills into what orbits it, what sits on its surface, and what has been charted within, all the way down to a single settlement — every entity page carries breadcrumbs back up the chain, fact cards, who and what is present there grouped by kind, relationships organized by category, and lore as an expandable reading list. Kaleidos gets a two-panel chart from the same coordinates: a surface map with latitude, longitude, adjacency, and settlement size classes, and a local orbital view with the ring band, span-linked stations tethered sunward, and route segments passing through. Worlds without authored coordinates keep the inferred layout. The chronicle wizard browses this same atlas to pick the opening location, and its anchor step groups candidates by kind with prominence badges.

summary: Added monthly player limits for model usage
details: Every model request now carries the player's Cognito username into Amazon Bedrock's request metadata and is checked against a calendar-month spending limit before invocation. Players receive a $10 monthly allowance, while members of the existing admin role receive $50. Concurrent requests reserve their estimated maximum cost transactionally, then replace that reservation with the provider's metered token cost so parallel turns cannot race past the limit.

summary: Closed chronicles now write their stories into world canon
details: When a chronicle closes, the archivist reviews its transcript and records the outcome in the world graph. Canon entities that were central to the story receive a lore fragment recording what happened to them, named people, places, and things the story invented become new world entities with their own founding lore, and relationships the story established become edges in the graph. Scenes guide the archive: whatever a dialog, battle, hunt, chase, or search revolved around is treated as significant, earning lore if it is already canon and priority consideration as a new entity if it is not. Play-born entities carry a living description recomputed from everything recorded about them, and grow in prominence as lore and connections accumulate. Generic props never qualify: a named sword can enter canon, a plain knife cannot.

summary: Character creation is a guided six-step build with real limits
details: The one-page character form is now a six-step wizard. You pick a species, culture, homeland and faction allegiance from world canon rather than typing them, and an archetype preset sets two advanced attributes and three skills for you to edit. Attributes and skills now have a budget — two attributes at advanced, an optional superior paid for with one rudimentary, and exactly three skills at one artisan and two apprentice — enforced in the form and again on the server, which now builds the character record itself instead of trusting the browser. Skills are written as actions rather than disciplines. The optional Nature step records callings, a drive, a flaw, a standing instinct and one unique fact; each one you fill in gives the GM something specific to use, and blank fields are fine. All of it reaches the GM: narration charges costs against your flaw, options are framed for and against your callings, and closing turns state where those callings ended up. Starting skill ratings also now apply correctly on the first roll, where a naming mismatch used to drop them to untrained.

summary: Conversations, battles, hunts, chases, and searches now play by their own rules
details: The GM now recognizes sustained scene types from ordinary typed play without commands or keyword triggers. Dialog scenes focus the interface on the person speaking and keep their name on every response; battles tighten checks and physical consequences; hunts track progress toward a quarry; chases keep distance and route changing; and searches distinguish active investigation from simple observation. Each type supplies its own narration, check, and completion rules while the existing intent system still handles whatever the player chooses to type. Scene context is saved on every turn so transcript history remains consistent after play moves on.

summary: The landing page now shows chronicle activity across the frontier
details: The Around the Frontier panel lists the most recently completed chronicles across all players, with the character who lived them, where the story ended, and the archivist's closing summary as the hook once it has been written. Members, moderators, and admins also see currently open chronicles; free-tier players receive only completed stories.

summary: Scene subjects now connect to the world graph
details: When typed play starts a conversation, battle, hunt, chase, or search, the GM now links its free-text subject to an existing person, creature, faction, place, vessel, or object when the match is clear. Exact names resolve directly; less literal references use Titan text embeddings stored in PostgreSQL and are ranked through the existing relationship graph. Local marginal entities resolve only nearby while renowned and mythic subjects remain recognizable farther across the graph. Uncertain and newly invented subjects remain valid free text instead of forcing a wrong match. Structured model responses now expose scene types, entity kinds, known beat IDs, and offered entity slugs as provider-checked values rather than unrestricted strings.

summary: Character and chronicle choices now come directly from canon
details: Species, cultures, homelands, allegiances, and chronicle locations now show only the choices selected by the world canon, with concise origin descriptions written for character creation. Chronicle locations offer direct local focus entities, including new one-sentence people and story hooks shared across related places. Reference articles remain available for background reading but no longer appear as people, places, or graph shortcuts, and hidden GM entries stay out of player-facing Atlas results.

summary: Expired sessions now refresh during play
details: The client now renews an expiring Cognito access token before its next API request, so a session can continue after the original token times out without a hard browser refresh. A readable unauthorized response still gets one refresh-and-retry attempt, while a session that can no longer be renewed returns to login instead of leaving the interface apparently signed in. On initial load, a neutral loading screen now remains visible while stored credentials are checked, then gives way to either the signed-in app or the login screen without flashing the wrong destination first.

summary: The landing page now follows new entities and lore
details: Two new dashboard panels show the world graph changing as chronicles enter canon. New Lore lists entities that recently received a lore fragment after their creation, including the fragment title and an excerpt. New Entities lists the latest people, places, factions, artifacts, and other entries added to the world. Every name opens its complete World Atlas entry, and hidden GM records and reference articles stay out of both feeds.

summary: Atlas charts now show everything that is charted
details: The Kaleidos System entry opens on the system chart instead of a bare relationship list. Body charts now cover the whole subtree: ring habitats are strung along their ring's band, trade-lane hubs appear at their authored offsets, zones like The Shear render as band segments instead of point markers, and satellites without recorded positions ride a visible dashed outer track rather than hiding in a footnote. Any body with orbiters gets a chart, so Vastine's moon is one click away. Trade routes draw brighter with haloed labels. Every entity now opens with an authored identity summary that says what the subject is, where it belongs, and what it does, without truncating or repeating the lead lore passage. Relationships already shown as breadcrumbs, chart children, or Present-here entries stay out of the relationship list, lore tags appear once instead of on every fragment, and same-titled passages get a distinguishing excerpt. The chronicle wizard's location step is now a pure drill-down map: click a body to descend into its orbit and surface, keep descending through rings, regions, and settlements via cluster views, and click a glowing place to choose it as the opener. A breadcrumb trail and an Up button climb back out, a context strip describes the body in view and offers a Start-at button when that body can itself host the chronicle, the chosen place carries a gold ring and label on every chart level, and a persistent bar under the chart spells out where the chronicle opens — nothing is pre-chosen for you. Planetary surfaces now render as a globe: an orthographic disc turned toward the charted face, with a graticule, rim labels on leader lines, and adjacency edges, replacing the flat coordinate box. Opening the sun shows the system chart instead of an empty body view, and chart captions drop the importer jargon. Drilling into any contained place — a surface region, a city, a hab interior — now shows terrain instead of a mock orbit: an outlined stretch of ground with the place's name set across it and its sites marked inside, so Sable Crescent reads as a river basin with Thornvault and Ledgerfall in it rather than a planet with moons. Picking a location no longer bounces the layout: the loading banners are gone, replaced by a small spinner in a fixed slot beside Refresh. Places charted without a position, including ones created during play, appear as adrift markers at the foot of the system chart. Lore sections stopped mixing registers: the one-line annotations that relationships carry now sit in their own compact Relationship-notes list instead of masquerading as same-titled lore passages, lore prose renders its markdown with cross-references resolved to atlas links where the target exists, and summary-versus-lore duplicate detection sees through those links.

summary: Established world entities are now part of ordinary play
details: Each chronicle now keeps a small stable roster of nearby, scene-relevant, connected, and recently involved entities. The compact roster sits beside the chronicle, shows concrete people, organizations, creatures, vehicles, artifacts, usable resources, specific places, incidents, and rumors, and opens each entity's current Atlas record without interrupting play. Chronicle setup uses that same concrete-entity rule for anchor choices, so anything selected as the story's premise can also appear in its live roster. Article-like species, eras, concepts, materials, forgotten entities, and world-scale locations remain available to free-text reference resolution without being proactively offered or presented as anchors. Players interact through typed prose; ordinary names, aliases, and clear vague references resolve against established entities. Resolved references in player and GM transcript text are underlined and open a compact Atlas preview. The GM receives private authored usage notes only after an entity enters context, can ignore irrelevant entities or apply a note without forcing a name into the prose, and gives the strongest continuity weight to entities the player actually addresses. Chronicle closure now considers referenced entities rather than everything that happened to be displayed.

summary: Completed chronicles can no longer be resumed
details: Completed chronicles remain visible in chronicle lists, but their Resume and Load actions are now replaced by a disabled Completed state. This prevents a finished story from being reactivated while keeping its completion status visible.

summary: The GM can now invent on the world's unfinished hooks
details: Nearly half the world's canon entities were published as hooks: a name, a single suggestive line, and no detail behind them. The GM could not tell them apart from fully written canon, so it treated a blank as settled fact and narrated around it. Those hooks are now marked for the GM as long as no chronicle has established anything about them, and the GM is told to invent them concretely on contact and hold that invention for the rest of the story. The first chronicle to make something of a hook turns it into ordinary canon that later stories must respect. At most two hooks appear among the seven nearby entities a chronicle offers, so play always has both settled ground to stand on and new ground to claim.

summary: Canon refreshes now remove retired material
details: Each supplied canon revision now replaces the previous imported snapshot. Entities, lore fragments, and relationships removed from the source are deleted from the game database instead of lingering in the Atlas or narrative context, while records created through play remain intact unless they belong to a removed entity.

summary: GM prompt edits now reach the running game
details: Every GM instruction existed in three places: the template files, a copy inside the database seed, and a few hand-written patches in a schema migration. The seed reapplied itself on each release and overwrote the others, so four templates had been edited without any of those edits ever affecting play — including the rules that keep the narrator from inventing your character's actions, the guidance for naming a new skill, and how a chronicle's closing turn resolves. The templates are now the only place an instruction is written, the database is loaded from them on every release, and a test fails if the two ever disagree. Personal template overrides are unaffected and continue to take precedence over the official wording.

summary: The chronicle's goal is now a living thing
details: Every chronicle now begins with its seed as the founding beat, so the story's initial goal is tracked from turn one instead of living outside the beat system. Beats gained two new endings alongside success and failure: a beat is superseded when a newer goal replaces it as the story's direction, and abandoned when play has genuinely walked away from it — a quiet beat stays open, and the GM sees when each beat last advanced so slow-burn threads survive. The chronicle only closes on its own when its open beats are resolved, and the closing archivist reads the full goal history: earned arcs become lore, superseded beats show where the story turned, abandoned threads stay unresolved. Beat tracking is no longer optional; the wizard toggle is gone.

summary: The left rail now follows what you are doing
details: The app now has one left-rail position with two mutually exclusive scopes. Outside play, the main rail holds character and chronicle directories plus their creation, resume, and delete actions. Inside a chronicle, it is replaced by a story rail containing the active character and chronicle controls, beats, and nearby entities. The landing dashboard no longer repeats the two directories.

summary: The GM now keeps a notebook, and scenes have clocks
details: The GM maintains a working memory of the current scene — what kind of place it is, who is present, and what just happened — and writes every narration against it, so a hostel stays a hostel and people stay where they were left. A read-only GM Notebook panel in the chronicle overview shows it. Scenes now carry a visible progress clock that skill checks move, and a full clock means the scene resolves rather than dragging on; a scene whose premise dissolves is closed as abandoned instead of following the story around. Battles are detected from combat itself, destinations must be real places the prose actually reaches, and items the story puts in your hands now land in your inventory. Failed turns show a clear notice instead of narration whose effects never happened, and blocked content asks for a rephrase instead of leaking a filter message. When a chronicle closes, any beat left open receives an honest final disposition — succeeded, failed, or abandoned — before the story and canon are written.

summary: GM turns respond faster
details: The engine behind each turn made up to a dozen separate model calls, several of them re-reading the same context. Beat targeting now rides inside the intent classification instead of its own call, and the four post-narration judgments — summary, beats, the scene notebook, and location — are made together in a single pass, which also means they can no longer contradict one another. A typical turn now makes about half the classification calls it used to and resolves noticeably faster.

summary: Generated seeds are written for your character
details: Seed generation now reads your character sheet — drive, flaw, origin, allegiance, and skills — alongside the location and anchor lore, and each hook must implicate that character specifically and state a goal worth pursuing, since the seed you pick becomes the chronicle's founding beat. Seeds are also written by the prose model instead of the lightweight classifier. The seed prompt was rebuilt around a strict process-and-data format, and every GM prompt now keeps its instructions fixed while the story data arrives in clearly labeled blocks, a structure enforced by tests. The beat panels no longer claim beats appear only after the first turn.

summary: Atlas links now keep your place
details: Entity names throughout the dashboard, chronicle rail, location display, transcript references, lore, and Atlas relationships now open the referenced Atlas entry in a dialog instead of replacing the current screen or opening a new tab. Every link still points to the entity's readable slug URL, so it can be copied, opened in a new tab, or expanded into the full Atlas page without finding an internal ID.

summary: Turns work again, and prompt updates actually ship
details: A recent restructuring left the deploy unable to deliver prompt template updates, so production kept old prompts and every turn failed after its narration streamed, showing both a GM response and an error notice. The deploy now regenerates the prompt seed before uploading it, restoring the missing turn-judge prompt and putting all current prompts — now in a consistent role, process, and data-legend format — live. Moderator diagnostics also gained read access to the LLM audit tables.

summary: Compare candidate GM narrators on every turn
details: Each turn now also runs a panel of experimental GM narrators that search world canon, relationships, lore, and chronicle history themselves before writing, instead of receiving a pre-selected slice. Expanded GM messages gain a pager to cycle between the current narrator's response and each panel response, labeled by model. The story is still driven only by the current narrator; turns may take longer while the panel runs. The GM's narration prompts have been restored to their earlier, terser wording on every path after the reformatted versions produced flatter, more generic prose. One panel model that kept rewriting failed rolls as successes has been retired, so the panel is now two narrators instead of three.

summary: Stop every turn from piling on new trouble
details: The GM prepares several possible complications before a roll and used to play all of them no matter how the roll went, so even a success ended with fresh problems and a run of bad luck spiralled with no way out. A turn that goes badly now brings one complication, and a turn that goes well brings none. The GM also tracks its story goals more honestly: a turn spent on something the current goal never asked for no longer counts as progress toward it, and a fight or conversation that is already several turns old can now be recognized as a scene instead of going untracked.

summary: Name the chronicle, character, and player in audit review
details: The moderator audit queue identified every request by raw id, so finding the turn you cared about meant recognizing a uuid. The queue and the review dialog now show the chronicle title, character name, and player name instead. Names are resolved when a record is read, so the entire existing audit history reads back named and a later rename shows up everywhere at once.

summary: The GM looks things up before it writes
details: Turns are now written in two passes. A scout searches world canon, relationships, lore, and past turns for what this particular turn needs, then hands the storyteller a short brief: what it found, who is present and what they want, what is at stake, and the complication when a roll goes badly. The storyteller writes from that brief alone, so the prose is no longer competing with a catalogue of world data it never asked for. The world material offered to the GM is now only what the turn actually touches — a chronicle about hunting in a gas giant no longer carries a pilgrim bead and a guild charter around with it. Rolls are much rarer: they are there for tension, not to adjudicate every sentence. Scenes now track what is at stake, what would end them, and whether anything changed, so a scene that has stalled can be recognized as stalled.

summary: The world does things you did not cause
details: Until now every event in a chronicle was a reaction to something you had just done: the jam happened because you fired, the vortex opened because you accelerated. The GM now takes a turn as the world before your action is weighed — the people elsewhere, the factions, the machinery all get to act on what they want, out of what canon already says about them. What they are doing is recorded on every turn whether or not the narration shows it, so something that stirs quietly now can arrive later. Behind that, the GM keeps up to three running agendas with clocks; when a clock fills, that thing happens. Your action always resolves exactly as you described it — what changes is the situation you are standing in when it does. Scenes also stop needing dice to move: a conversation or a search that genuinely got somewhere now advances the scene. At the All visibility level you can see the world's turn and its clocks under each GM reply.

summary: Character choices now look selected
details: Species, culture, homeland, allegiance, standing, archetype, and attribute choices now switch from muted gray to a filled teal treatment with a bright border when selected. The larger choice cards also show a check mark, while keyboard focus keeps its separate visible ring.

summary: One way of showing the world to the GM
details: The chronicle opening and the turn engine each had their own way of describing a place to the model, and only one of them was ever maintained. The opening was still shipping your character's species, culture, homeland, and allegiance as raw identifiers, five entire lore articles for a single location with the same tags repeated in each, and Atlas links written into the prose. Both now go through one description of an entity, so a fix reaches every prompt at once. That description leads with the canon's own summary of a place or person — its setting, what happens there, and what makes it dangerous — with lore kept as short entries underneath instead of the other way around, and it carries the GM notes an entry publishes, which the opening never saw at all. Those summaries had been written for two days without ever reaching the game: the deploy recognized a canon refresh only by the revision it was imported from, so a rebuild of the same revision looked like nothing had changed. It now recognizes the canon by what is in it, and this release carries the waiting refresh — descriptive summaries for 237 entries, two new entries, and nineteen new lore passages, visible in the Atlas as well as to the GM.

summary: The GM reads the world before it writes about it
details: Turns are written in two passes: one that looks things up and one that writes. The looking-up pass was handing the writing pass six one-line notes, and the writing pass was also being given the same raw character sheet, location line, and scene roster the first pass had already read — two sources for one scene, which is how a chronicle about you ended up narrating an NPC gathering his tools while you worked. Now there is one author for each thing. The writer keeps what a retelling would damage: your own words, the roll, the scene's clock, what you are carrying, and the reply it wrote last turn. Everything that takes judgement — who you are in this world and what your species, culture, homeland, and allegiance actually mean for you here; where you are standing and what that place does to a person in it; who is with you and what they want; what has happened that bears on now — is read out of world canon and written for the storyteller in prose. Looking a place up now returns everything the entry holds instead of the few fields the GM thought to ask for, and when you refer back to something from earlier the GM searches the chronicle for what actually happened rather than repeating your phrasing back to you.

summary: The GM researches your turn before writing it, and keeps what it finds
details: Three failures from live play, fixed together. First: when you named something the world's index didn't list — a machine you coined a name for two turns ago — the GM's lookup reported the miss as if it were a fact of the world, and that report could end up in the narration's source material. A miss is now an error the GM recovers from: it searches the canon under other wordings and searches the chronicle's own past turns, where player-named things actually live, before treating anything as new. Search itself also stopped pretending: it used to return the five nearest entries no matter how unrelated they were, so an invented word came back looking like five matches; results below a measured similarity floor now count as no match at all. Second: the research pass could do all its reading and then lose everything on delivery — one field of its report shaped wrong discarded the whole thing, and the writer got an empty stand-in. The valid fields now survive. Third: the research pass itself is held to the job. Its instructions now define done as a brief a stranger to this world could write the scene from, calibrate how much looking a routine turn takes, and require the character sheet's grades to arrive exactly as written — a turn where your rudimentary presence became "advanced" is the failure this guards against. Retrieval calls now run deterministically, and every turn opens by reading before writing.

summary: The world stops narrating you and starts moving on its own
details: The GM's world stage — the pass that decides what everything that is not you is doing — was reading your message, your character sheet, and your intent before deciding, and it answered them: its first agenda in a chronicle was your own task with your name on it, and its world line each turn restated whatever you had just done. It no longer sees you at all. It receives the world's own material — the agendas already running, what canon says about the place and the figures pursuing those agendas, the last narration, and its own record of what the world has been doing — and continues that motion. The canon it needs is fetched for it directly instead of hoping it goes looking, so a city whose repair lines are shut becomes an agenda with a named faction rather than weather. An agenda proposed for something that does not exist in canon is discarded instead of tracked, which is the door your own character came through.

summary: Resume an active chronicle from an earlier turn
details: Every newly completed turn in an active chronicle now offers Resume from here. Confirming it creates the next version of that chronicle, copies its transcript through the selected turn, and restores the story's location, scenes, beats, nearby entities, and world agendas as they stood there. The original remains unchanged, later versions are named v2, v3, and onward, and completed chronicles cannot branch. Characters are never copied or rewound: every version points to the same character record and shares its current progression. Existing chronicles can branch from their current tip after this update; their older turns predate the exact story checkpoints and do not offer the action.

summary: The GM's research runs under a judge instead of grading itself
details: The pass that reads the world before your turn used to decide for itself when it had read enough, and the same call that would have had to do more work was the call allowed to declare the work done — so it stopped early, reliably, on every model we run. Research is now split from judgment: one invocation retrieves, a separate one inspects everything actually retrieved and either closes the research or names what is still missing, and those gaps drive the next round of retrieval. The brief itself moved out of a tool call: models write measurably worse prose inside escaped JSON arguments, and both of ours had been failing there — one wrote a field as prose where the schema wanted structure, the other abandoned the tool call entirely. The brief is now composed as plain labeled prose, the format models write well, and a small second step files it into the schema. Tool results also stopped arriving as escaped JSON, every tool now says when it should and should not be used, and nothing forces a tool call anymore — forcing turns off the tool-selection reasoning both providers document as load-bearing.

summary: The comparison panel measures retrieval instead of a second model
details: The panel beside each turn used to run a whole second research pass on a cheaper model. It never finished its own research — it asked for the same things round after round and always ran out its budget rather than concluding — and what it produced answered a question nobody had, since it varied the model and the context at once. It is now a single alternate written by the same model that wrote your turn, on a world assembled without any searching: the story's anchors and place are walked outward through canon's own relationships, your words are matched against canon by meaning to reach what that walk cannot, and everything found is handed over at once, along with how those things stand with each other. The remaining difference between the two responses is retrieval, which is the comparison worth reading. It also cuts roughly forty percent of the work each turn was doing.

summary: Two fields the models were reading as the wrong question
details: The pass that decides what the world is doing had one field with no description on it, sitting beside blocks naming your location — and on later turns it began answering it as a location, returning the place name where three sentences of what the world was doing belonged. Those turns lost the world's account of itself entirely. The field now says what it wants. Separately, the research pass reads canon passages by a handle it gets back from searching, and that handle was labeled with the same word as an entity's name, so the model kept feeding passage handles to the tool that opens entities: half of all failed lookups in a recent chronicle were this one mistake. The two are now named apart.

summary: Pick up to three prose models and compare them side by side
details: Player settings now takes a primary, a secondary, and a tertiary prose model. The primary writes the turns your chronicle keeps and nothing else changes about it. A secondary or tertiary writes nothing canonical: each one appears twice in the comparison panel beside the turn — once having researched the world through the retrieval loop, once handed the world whole with no searching at all. Reading down the panel compares models on the same scene; reading across one model's pair shows what retrieval was worth to it. Both extra slots default to None, which is the off switch: leave them there and a turn costs exactly what it costs today. Classification is unchanged and stays on one model, because every classification call sits on the turn's critical path and a second opinion would decide nothing. The panel's cost now charges that classification step at the classifier's actual rate instead of attributing all of the turn's tokens to the prose model.

summary: Five open-weight models, and Nova's price was wrong
details: GPT OSS 120B and 20B, Kimi K2 Thinking, Qwen3 Next 80B, and Qwen3 32B are now selectable. Every one was checked against Bedrock directly rather than taken on reputation: all are on-demand in this region, all handle tool use through the same interface the retrieval loop uses, and all honor a forced tool choice, which is how structured output is produced. Prices come from AWS's own pricing service. Several are genuinely cheaper than what was on offer — GPT OSS 120B costs a fifth of Nova Pro per million input tokens and Qwen3 32B a fifth of its output — though Kimi K2 Thinking is not: its output runs above Nova Pro's. MiniMax M2.5 was measured and left out because it ignores a forced tool choice, which would break structured output. The catalog's Nova prices were also twice the real rate on output for both Nova Pro and Nova 2 Lite, so cost reporting had been overstating them. The deployed narrative and canon services now have Bedrock permission for every selectable model and the Cohere index they search.

summary: Canon search now scores whether an entry answers you, not whether it sounds like you
details: Searching canon by meaning used to put your words and the world's entries into one space and measure how alike the two sentences were. But canon reads "Heat-road haulers carry bulk freight between Ashvane towns" while you ask "what's moving the cargo out here" — those answer each other without resembling each other. Canon and queries are now embedded separately by a model trained for exactly that asymmetry, at four times the previous detail. The improvement is measurable: against four hundred real canon entries, ten plain-language questions now find the right entry nine times out of ten, where the old thresholds would have discarded six of them as noise. Every cutoff in the system was re-measured against the new model rather than carried over — the old numbers were tuned for the old one and would have rejected correct matches, including a fifth of scene subjects and a sixth of the things you name directly. Invented words are still rejected: thirteen nonsense phrases were tested and none scored high enough to come back as canon. Existing canon is re-indexed automatically; until that finishes, searching by meaning returns nothing rather than something wrong. Scene-subject matching now applies its measured cutoff in one place, so candidates between the new and old floors reach the resolver instead of disappearing inside the index.

summary: The world can start something with someone nobody wrote down yet
details: The pass that decides what the world is doing on its own account could only ever hand an agenda to a figure already written into canon — a rule added to stop it handing one to you, which it did once. The cost was a world that could never introduce the night crew, the rival office, or the machine that turns out to matter, so everything happening offstage had to be traceable to something already indexed. It can now name a figure of its own and start them going; the only thing it still may not do is run your agenda. It has also been told plainly what belongs there: a lift that comes down out of sequence, a route whose readings changed, a shift that never clocked off — motion that isn't about you, that you may never learn the cause of, and that the story can later turn out to have needed. Your own work disturbing something offstage is now a reason for that thing to move, not a reason to leave it out.

summary: New story threads get named instead of quietly ignored
details: The turn judge was told to hold off on starting a new story beat whenever it was unsure, and it duly started none — a recent chronicle ran three turns in which a dimensional key was built and revealed to the one person who could act on it, and the only beat recorded was the one the chronicle opened with. It is now told the cost runs the other way: naming a beat that later goes quiet costs a line in a list, while failing to name one costs the arc. When a turn changes what the story is about and no open beat covers it, that thread gets a name. The scene notebook also has to list whoever you are speaking to by name — a scene whose other party was missing read to every later turn as a room you were standing in alone.

summary: Fixed silent stage failures that emptied the GM's research
details: Several stages hand back a structured record rather than prose, and they were asked for it in prose — "answer continue", "report the gaps" — with the tool they were meant to call described only as "extract structured data matching the schema". Given a full-sized turn, models did what they were asked and wrote the answer out in prose, which the engine could not read, so the stage failed and the turn continued with an empty research brief. In one chronicle that happened four times across three turns, and the resulting ungrounded narration was then treated as established fact by the next turn's research. Every structured stage now names the call it must make and says that the call is the whole response. Measured against real turn-sized inputs, this took compliance from 4 in 12 to 12 in 12 on the affected models.

summary: The dice now tell the GM what happened in a sentence, and complications come from the world
details: A resolved check used to reach the GM as a single word — advance, regress, collapse — beside an instruction to honor it. Nothing in any of the thirty-one prompts ever said what those five words mean, so the GM was asked to honor a scale it had never been shown and guessed from the word itself; in a recent chronicle a catastrophic failure was narrated as a triumph because 'collapse', in a room full of resonant screens, reads as something falling over. The result now arrives as one plain sentence saying what the check did to what your character was reaching for, with their recent run of luck and the odds they faced folded into it. How that lands is still entirely the GM's to write. Separately, the pre-written complications are gone: they were drafted before the dice by a stage that had read nothing about the world, which is why failure so often arrived as a convenient tremor or a passing patrol. The complication is now written after the outcome is known by whichever stage has actually read the setting — so what goes wrong belongs to this place and these people.

summary: The GM stops reading the rulebook out loud, and a failed research pass says why
details: One narrator wrote your 'fledgling negotiate deals skill' straight into the story. The rule against naming the machinery — drive, flaw, instinct, skill, check, tier, momentum — existed in exactly one of the thirteen prompts that write prose; it is now in all of them, and the line describing how a roll went no longer quotes the skill's internal name either. Separately, when the GM's research pass fails the turn still continues on what it has, but the record of that failure said only 'Error' with no further detail, and reported the work as though none had been done — so a pass that searched and lost its findings looked identical to one that never searched. It now names the stage that failed and what it rejected, keeps the honest count of what was retrieved, and marks the resulting narration so the two can be told apart.

summary: Turns stop failing because a model ran out of room to think
details: Every stage of a turn had a hard ceiling on how much it could produce, and those ceilings were set small — small enough that a model which thinks before it answers spent the whole allowance thinking and returned nothing usable. That is what failed a turn outright with 'the turn could not be completed', and what silently emptied the GM's research on one of the three models every single turn. The ceilings are now generous everywhere and are clamped automatically to whatever each model actually supports; how long an answer should be is stated in the instructions, where a model can read it, instead of enforced by a cutoff it cannot see. Research also became best-effort: if the pass that judges whether enough has been found fails, the turn is now written from whatever was already retrieved rather than throwing all of it away. And the error records that hid all of this behind the single word 'Error' now carry the actual reason.

summary: The GM stops arguing with things you said you did
details: You wrote that you cast a ward, and the GM replied 'You didn't cast Ward—you never do.' A GM may decide your attempt failed; it may never decide it didn't happen. When you name a capability, a device, or a piece of craft the world has never written down, it is yours and it is real, and the narration now has to say what it does. The same instinct was making the GM's research chase its own tail: it treated every name you invented as a missing piece of world lore and spent its whole research budget hunting for a definition that was never going to exist. A name with no history is simply new — the story is free to make it, and the research moves on.

summary: Turn summaries record the roll instead of guessing at it
details: A turn that went badly was being logged as '(it worked)', because the part of the engine that writes the one-line summary had been asked to judge the outcome from how the narration read — and narration about a discovery reads like success even when the dice said otherwise. It now copies the recorded result instead of interpreting it. Story beats also get another push: the judge is asked outright what the story now owes an ending that it didn't owe before this turn, and told not to talk itself out of the answer because the chronicle's opening premise could be stretched to cover it. Comparison panels also record which model wrote each one, which they previously did not.

summary: New default models: quicker bookkeeping, better prose
details: The work a turn does behind the narration — classifying what you attempted, planning the roll, recording what changed, tracking your inventory — accounts for around thirty seconds of every turn. That work now runs on Amazon Nova Lite, measured at 3.4 seconds against the previous default's 4.2 on the heaviest of those calls, and costing a fraction as much. Narration now defaults to Kimi K2 Thinking, which wrote the strongest prose across every chronicle we compared: concrete images, endings that hand you a choice instead of a portent, and the fewest lapses into restating what you just typed. Both defaults apply to new players. If you have already chosen your own models in settings, your choices are untouched.

summary: The World Guide now carries the ordinary life of the setting
details: The new Encyclopedia adds creatures, resources, abilities, technologies, roles, cultures, and recurring phenomena beside the Atlas's named people and places. Chronicle creation and the live left rail show a collapsible Common here field guide for the current location. Click an entry to read it; during play, double-click or right-click any Atlas or Encyclopedia item to attach it to your next move. The GM searches both catalogs and Chronicle history through one reference system, while the Encyclopedia remains suggestive rather than exhaustive — unlisted inventions are still welcome. Species and culture now come from this reusable catalog, and narrated Encyclopedia terms open the same World Guide as Atlas references. Character drafts saved before this update now reset cleanly instead of crashing when their obsolete origin selections are loaded.
